articles.headline: Why is Speculative Decoding Fast?
articles.blurb: Speculative Decoding is a technique where a small draft model proposes a likely draft sequence, and a big model verifies that sequence in parallel in a single forward pass. It enables the ability to look at many tokens at once and accept the ones that would have been generated by the big model. When the batch size is smaller than the optimal number of tokens, speculative decoding allows models to use 'free' compute to complete sequences faster. However, at high throughput, you could actually be wasting compute when you could be using that time to move memory.

The Ethereum roadmap already targets hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification, and Drake is pushing to accelerate those timelines, while advising oracles and L2 security councils to rotate ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message.

articles.headline: Vitalik on AI-Accelerated Cryptography: Hash-Based Over Lattices
articles.blurb: Vitalik Buterin warns that AI-accelerated mathematical research may erode the security of lattice-based cryptography (ML-DSA, LWE, and FHE) through the same mechanism that GNFS degraded RSA, where decades of optimization shrunk effective key strength by an order of magnitude, and projects that AI could compress 50 years of math progress into two years. Ethereum's lean roadmap has already pivoted to hash-only signatures (WOTS and SPHINCS+), dropping lattices, ML-DSA, Falcon, and lattice-based commitments from ZK proofs. Public-key encryption cannot be constructed from hashes alone due to long-standing mathematical constraints, which means secure messaging, VPNs, and anonymizing protocols face an open problem that extends well beyond blockchains. Buterin's practical recommendations include keeping funds in addresses that have not yet broadcast transactions, moving multisig confirmations offchain to avoid exposing signer public keys, and routing encrypted notes through offchain channels rather than publishing them onchain.

articles.headline: Navi Pillay awarded Peace Prize: 'Lifetime spent fighting for what's right & to uphold human rights'
articles.blurb: Haxie Meyers-Belkin is pleased to welcome Rosa Freedman, Professor of Law Conflict and Global Development at the University of Reading. Navi Pillay's career represents a remarkable contribution to international law and human rights, from her pioneering role in post-apartheid South Africa to her work at the United Nations. Yet her legacy also raises difficult questions about political impartiality, particularly in relation to Israel and Gaza. She believes we need to distinguish between the significance of her lifelong achievements and the controversy surrounding the decision to award her the Nobel Peace Prize at this particular moment. More broadly, this debate invites us to examine whether the prize is recognising individual merit or increasingly serving as a vehicle for political messaging. At a time when international law and multilateral institutions face mounting pressure, and serious threats, Freedman asserts that the challenge is to scrutinise their shortcomings without undermining the principles they exist to uphold.
